国民经济电力工业系列文集|书籍和编辑卷| 2026 年 11 月 16 日 | ITIF跳到内容
国民经济电力工业系列文集
中国主导战略重要产业的系统性运动如何威胁美国的技术领先地位、经济实力和国家安全，以及美国政策制定者应该采取什么措施。
信息技术与创新基金会 (ITIF) 进行了为期 18 个月的研究，探讨中国霸道的产业战略如何威胁美国的技术领先地位、经济实力和国家安全。 ITIF 的研究得出的结论是，美国政策制定者必须从根本上改变该国的科技工业经济体系，以防止美国在为 21 世纪国家实力提供基础的关键先进贸易部门行业中屈服于中国。 ITIF 将这些行业称为“国民经济动力行业”。
这项研究工作于 2025 年 11 月至 2026 年 11 月期间产生了一系列 19 份政策报告。
该系列的第一份报告全面概述了中国正在发动的技术经济贸易战，以牺牲美国及其西方盟友的利益来主导这些行业。
第二组九份报告包括对美国工业表现与中国在国民经济实力行业方面的定量和定性分析。
第三组共九份报告，为美国政策制定者提供了近 200 条具体建议，以重组政府并动员起来应对与中国的技术经济贸易战。
这些报告可以连续提供，也可以作为选集提供：
随后是概述报告的执行摘要以及 ITIF 政策建议索引。
中国正在系统性地主导先进产业，从而在 21 世纪增强国家实力，美国面临着生存挑战。与美国历史上的任何竞争对手不同，中国将拥有 14 亿人口的大陆经济规模与明确致力于实现对西方民主世界的技术经济优势的马克思列宁主义政治体系结合起来。这不是市场经济体之间的正常经济竞争，而是一场精心策划的、长达数十年的战略运动，旨在取代美国的工业能力、削弱盟国，并从根本上重塑中共领导下的全球秩序。
其中的利害关系超越了经济范畴。今天的国家实力取决于本报告所称的“国家电力工业”的实力，这些部门涵盖纯粹的国防生产、军事和商业应用中使用的军民两用技术，以及支持更广泛工业公域的赋能产业。其中包括半导体、航空航天、生物制药、电信设备、先进化学品、精密机械、机器人、人工智能（AI）系统以及其他数十个领域，在这些领域，企业实力减弱或受到致命伤害将赋予中国对美国及其盟国的危险影响力，并削弱美国的国防生产能力。
按照目前的发展轨迹，中国很可能很快就会在国家电力行业积累比美国大得多的能力。
这场竞争是在美国政策失败的背景下发生的。二十多年来，美国两党领导人一直在努力

National Economic Power Industry Series Anthology
How China’s systematic campaign to dominate strategically important industries threatens America’s technological leadership, economic strength, and national security—and what U.S. policymakers should do about it.
The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF) has conducted an 18-month research effort examining how China’s domineering industrial strategy threatens U.S. technological leadership, economic strength, and national security. ITIF’s research concludes that U.S. policymakers must fundamentally transform the country’s techno-industrial economic system to prevent America from becoming subservient to China in a critical group of advanced, traded-sector industries that provide the foundation for national power in the 21st century. ITIF calls these industries “national economic power industries.”
This research effort produced a series of 19 policy reports from November 2025 through November 2026.
The first report in the series provides a comprehensive overview of the unfolding techno-economic-trade war that China is waging to dominate these industries at the expense of the United States and its allies in the West.
A second group of nine reports includes quantitative and qualitative analyses of U.S. industrial performance versus China in national economic power industries.
A third group of nine reports offers nearly 200 specific recommendations for U.S. policymakers to reorganize government and mobilize for the techno-economic-trade war with China.
The reports are available both serially and as an anthology:
An executive summary of the overview report follows, along with an index of ITIF’s policy recommendations.
The United States faces an existential challenge in China’s systematic campaign to dominate the advanced industries that enable national power in the 21st century. Unlike any competitor in American history, China combines the continental scale of a 1.4-billion-person economy with a Marxist-Leninist political system explicitly committed to achieving techno-economic supremacy over the Western democratic world. This is not normal economic competition between market economies—it is a carefully orchestrated, multi-decade strategic campaign to displace U.S. industrial capabilities, weaken allied nations, and fundamentally reshape the global order under CCP leadership.
The stakes transcend economics. National power today depends on strength in what this report terms “national power industries”—a spectrum of sectors spanning pure defense production, dual-use technologies employed in both military and commercial applications, and enabling industries that support the broader industrial commons. These include semiconductors, aerospace, biopharmaceuticals, telecommunications equipment, advanced chemicals, precision machinery, robotics, artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and dozens of other sectors in which weakened or fatally injured firms would grant China dangerous leverage over the United States and its allies, as well as weaken U.S. defense production capabilities.
On its current trajectory, it is likely that China will soon amass significantly greater capabilities than the United States will in national power industries.
This competition occurs against a backdrop of American policy failure. For over two decades, U.S. leaders across both parties have operated under the assumption that China was becoming a “normal” market economy that would gradually liberalize politically and economically. That assumption has proven catastrophically wrong. China today is more authoritarian, more aggressive internationally, and more committed to state-directed capitalism than at any point since Mao’s death.
On its current trajectory, it is likely that China will soon amass significantly greater capabilities than the United States will in national power industries. With those greater capabilities will come geostrategic hegemony over the West, unless the United States forestalls that outcome by adopting a new, transformative national power industry strategy that goes beyond a mere competitiveness or national innovation strategy. This is not a war that the United States and allies can win in the sense of significantly weakening or retarding the growth of China’s own national power industries. The only way Chinese attacks will end is if China becomes a free, democratic country. But the United States and allies can avoid defeat—keeping their national power industries relatively strong—by working together and adopting national power industry strategies.
Understanding the Chinese Communist Party’s True Objectives
Perhaps the most damning evidence of Chinese intentions comes from internal Communist Party documents and speeches intended for party members rather than foreign audiences. As China scholar Daniel Tobin has documented, these reveal a regime explicitly committed to Marxist-Leninist global ambitions that go far beyond merely moving up the value chain and growing its economy.
Xi Jinping has repeatedly framed China’s rise in ideological terms, stating that “scientific socialism is full of vitality in 21st century China” and that China offers “a new option for other countries and nations who want to speed up their development while preserving their independence.” In a 2013 speech to senior party officials, Xi declared that “the viewpoint of historical materialism that capitalism is doomed to failure and socialism will prevail” remains valid, and that China must “seize the initiative, win the competitive edge, and secure our future” in a “long-term cooperation and rivalry between the two social systems.”
Documents from the party’s 20th Congress state that China’s success has “significantly shifted the worldwide historical evolution of the contest between the two different ideologies and social systems of socialism and capitalism in a way that favors socialism.” Chinese leaders explicitly describe their work as part of a “great struggle” and “systems contest with Western capitalist democracy,” using terminology that leaves no ambiguity about their intentions.
On technology and industry specifically, party documents are equally explicit. The minister of Science and Technology wrote in the People’s Daily that “the scientific and technological revolution and the contest between major powers are intertwined; the high-tech field has become the forefront and main battlefield of international competition.” Another official commentary stated: “To a certain extent, those who gain access to the Internet will gain the world. Core technology is an important weapon for the country.”
China’s Made in China 2025 plan, while officially downplayed after international backlash, clearly articulates the goal: “Building an internationally competitive manufacturing industry is the only way China can enhance its comprehensive national strength, ensure national security, and build itself into a world power.” The plan calls for China to “seize the commanding heights of a new round of competition in the manufacturing industry” and achieve innovation leadership “ranking first globally.”
The CCP follows a predictable playbook across industry after industry.
Leading Chinese scholar Lu Yongxiang stated in 2024 that “by 2035, ‘Made in China’ will surpass the United States and become the global leader,” noting this would thrust the world into a “new era”—explicitly referencing an era of Chinese dominance. These are not the words of a nation seeking merely to “catch up” or achieve “legitimate development.” They are the explicit articulation of a campaign for global advanced industrial hegemony.
China’s actions match its rhetoric. The CCP follows a predictable playbook across industry after industry. First, attract foreign investment by promising market access. Second, coerce technology transfer through joint venture requirements and other mechanisms—pressure the U.S. Trade Representative has characterized as “particularly intense.” Third, support domestic firms in copying and incorporating foreign technology while building indigenous capabilities through programs such as the 2006 Medium- and Long-term Program for Science and Technology Development, which identified 402 core technologies to master.
Fourth, carve out and protect the Chinese market for Chinese firms, excluding foreign competitors once domestic champions can reasonably serve the entire Chinese market. Fifth, provide massive subsidies—estimated at minimum 1.73 percent of Chinese gross domestic product (GDP) annually, or over $400 billion per year, though actual figures are likely far higher accounting for provincial and local support. Finally, support Chinese firms “going out” to capture global market share, particularly in developing nations through Belt and Road Initiative investments exceeding $1 trillion. These dwarf the minimal industrial subsidies the U.S. government (USG) provides.
The scale of Chinese subsidies dwarfs anything in Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) nations. A German institute found that in 2022, 99 percent of listed Chinese firms received direct government subsidies, with electric vehicle (EV) maker BYD alone receiving over $3.7 billion. Chinese industrial subsidies were 4.5 times greater than U.S. subsidies as a share of GDP. Combined with a chronically undervalued currency, suppressed domestic consumption, and closed markets, these subsidies have enabled Chinese firms to sell below cost for years or decades, systematically destroying foreign competitors’ market positions.
This is not to say that all Chinese efforts or innovation are win-lose. If China invents a cure for Alzheimer’s, the world benefits (assuming the United States or its allies would not also do so). But this would also reduce U.S. (and allied) strength in the pharmaceutical industry.
Overall, the policy debate about China is largely dominated by international relations scholars and experts, not business or industrial strategy experts. The former are aware of the global competition for leadership in advanced industries, but they largely see it as subservient to overall foreign policy considerations and goals. Moreover, few understand the operation of advanced industries, the nature of the competition, or the importance of barriers to entry and reentry. As such, the prevailing narratives largely ignore techno-economic and trade war implications and the implications for U.S. power.
Current U.S. thinking about China coalesces around three main strategic approaches, all of which are inadequate to the challenge.
The first camp, still influential in much of the U.S. foreign policy establishment, prioritizes maintaining cooperative relations with China, even in the face of CCP behavior that harms U.S. national power industry capabilities. These experts argue that China’s growth benefits global prosperity, that Chinese cooperation is essential for addressing climate change and other global challenges, and that confrontation risks becoming a catastrophic conflict.
A 2019 open letter signed by over 100 prominent scholars claimed that “we do not believe Beijing is an economic enemy or an existential national security threat” and argued that “the fear that Beijing will replace the United States as the global leader is exaggerated.”
This camp consistently minimizes Chinese malfeasance while emphasizing supposed benefits of engagement. They cite Chinese economic growth as driving global prosperity (ignoring that China’s persistent trade surpluses actually reduce GDP elsewhere). In arguing that cooperation is needed on issues such as climate change, pandemic response, and AI governance, they gloss over the question of why the United States should be the supplicant when China has equal or greater interest in addressing these challenges.
Their fundamental error is treating China as a partner rather than a strategic competitor. Engagers assume that continued dialogue and economic ties will moderate China’s behavior, when two decades of evidence proves otherwise. They prioritize the process of engagement over the substance of outcomes, accepting Chinese predatory practices as the price of maintaining access and conversation.
The Deniers: Wait for China’s Collapse or Assume Inherent U.S. Superiority
A second camp acknowledges China’s rise but counsels patience, predicting that internal contradictions will lead to Chinese economic stagnation or political crisis. These analysts point to demographic decline, the housing bubble, government debt, and the inefficiencies of state capitalism as harbingers of inevitable Chinese failure. To be sure, many advance the well-trodden prescriptions such as improved K-12 education, more high-skill immigration, smarter regulation, and more government spending on science. But they will not go so far as to support a national power industry strategy.
This “Peak China” thesis is seductive because it requires no painful U.S. policy changes. If China is destined to collapse under its own weight, the United States need only wait and maintain its existing approaches to the economy, trade, and national security. Proponents cite any negative Chinese economic news as evidence that their predictions are materializing, while ignoring continued Chinese gains in technological capabilities and global market share of advanced industries.
The fatal flaw is mistaking China for the Soviet Union. Unlike Soviet command economics, Chinese state capitalism has proven remarkably effective at generating growth and technological advancement. The CCP studied why the Soviet Union failed and adopted fundamentally different economic management—allowing market forces to operate within state-directed strategic frameworks rather than attempting to centrally plan everything.
Moreover, even if China faces economic headwinds from demographics or debt, these business-cycle challenges do not negate its structural advantages in the techno-economic competition. Chinese firms will continue benefiting from massive subsidies, protected markets, and patient capital regardless of GDP growth rates. Waiting for China to self-destruct while Chinese companies dismantle Western industries one after another is a prescription for defeat.
The Innovationists: Technology Will Save Us
The third camp acknowledges the challenge China presents but argues that American innovation superiority will enable the United States to prevail. These “dynamists” focus on deregulation, immigration reform, scientific research funding, and nurturing entrepreneurship—particularly in cutting-edge fields such as AI, quantum computing, and synthetic biology.
This view holds that the United States need not defend legacy industries because American innovators will create entirely new sectors and the United States will lead them. Why fight over solar panels or EVs when we can dominate AI and quantum? The prescription is to boost science funding, reduce regulatory barriers, import more STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math) talent, and trust that Silicon Valley-style innovation will deliver victory.
The problems with this strategy are multiple. First, with a few exceptions (e.g., AI), it is industry-agnostic—there is no guarantee that market-driven innovation will produce capabilities in sectors that matter most for national power. Second, the United States has repeatedly lost production of technologies it invented, from televisions to solar panels to batteries, as other nations have commercialized American discoveries. Innovation alone does not ensure domestic production or competitive strength.
Third, advanced defense systems increasingly rely on commercial technologies (spin-on rather than spin-off), making a strategy that abandons commercial sectors to China while hoping to maintain defense-only production unrealistic and prohibitively expensive. Fourth, the “industrial commons”—the ecosystem of suppliers, skilled workers, and manufacturing capabilities—erodes when industries disappear, making future innovation harder. Intel founder Andy Grove’s warning resonates: “Abandoning today’s ‘commodity’ manufacturing can lock you out of tomorrow’s emerging industry.”
Finally, China is not ceding emerging technologies. Chinese firms are competitive or leading in AI (see Alibaba, Baidu, and DeepSeek), quantum communications, commercial space, robotics, and biotechnology. The notion that the United States can retreat to “higher ground” in emerging tech while China dominates established industries ignores that Chinese firms are aggressively pursuing both.
Why Current U.S. Economic Policy Frameworks Fail
The deeper problem is that dominant U.S. economic doctrines are fundamentally mismatched to the era of national power industry competition.
The reigning paradigm in U.S. economic policymaking—which critics call “neoliberalism”—treats all industries as equivalent. Financial services and semiconductor fabrication are no different; both simply respond to market signals. The goal is to maximize consumer welfare through efficient resource allocation, which markets achieve better than governments do.
In this framework, Chinese subsidies (including low labor costs and lax environmental regulations) are gifts to American consumers (lower prices!), not strategic attacks. Trade deficits reflect American prosperity (we’re rich enough to buy foreign goods!), not industrial weakness. Offshoring production to China demonstrates smart capital allocation by U.S. firms seeking higher returns, not a national security vulnerability.
The reigning paradigm in U.S. economic policymaking—which critics call “neoliberalism”—treats all industries as equivalent.
Consumer welfare economics has no concept of strategic industries or national power. Its proponents argue that “countries don’t compete, only companies do” and that concerns about industrial structure reflect economically illiterate protectionism. The Peterson Institute epitomizes this view, arguing that U.S.-China trade is “clearly win-win” and that “Chinese companies have a right to compete with U.S. companies and succeed in any sector, including in high-tech.”
This doctrine might have been adequate when America faced no serious techno-economic competitor; it is catastrophically inadequate against China’s state capitalist predation. Markets have no inherent reason to preserve semiconductor fabrication, aerospace, or pharmaceutical production domestically. They are equally happy producing legal services, retail, and hospitality, none of which enable national power.
But the reality of this techno-economic and trade attack fundamentally undercuts the foundation of consumer welfare economics and exposes its inability to address the current challenge. If national power is the ultimate goal, not consumer welfare, then this doctrine fails, at least in guiding the share of the economy composed of national economic power industries. If a nation’s industrial mix is critical, then a doctrine that gives equal weight to potato chips and computer chips fails.
The ascendant alternative on the Left is equally unsuited to the challenge. Neo–New Dealism focuses on redistribution, social justice, and worker welfare overgrowth and competitiveness. Its industrial policy priorities are human services (childcare, eldercare), climate-focused sectors (renewable energy), and breaking up large corporations through aggressive antitrust.
While rhetorically supporting “industrial policy,” progressives’ actual agenda—drug price controls, restricting intellectual property (IP), mandating labor standards that limit automation, attacking profitable corporations as exploitative—systematically weakens the large advanced-technology firms that must serve as national champions against Chinese competitors.
Moreover, neo–New Dealism’s massive social spending agenda would consume the fiscal resources needed for strategic industrial investment. Its anticorporate ideology and deep suspicion of business-government collaboration make the public-private partnerships required for an effective national power industry strategy politically toxic.
The reality of the CCP’s techno-economic and trade war on the West undercuts the foundations of neo–New Deal progressivism. If the United States is in an existential contest for global power, then boosting taxes and regulations on business is especially ill-advised, as are the neo-Brandeisian campaign to destroy large corporations and separate unrestrained demands from organized labor. Progressive advocates know this quite well, which is why they go to any end to deny that China is even a competitor.
What’s Required: National Power Industry Strategy
The United States needs a fundamentally new framework: a national power industry strategy. This approach recognizes the following:
Industries differ fundamentally in strategic importance. Semiconductors and furniture are not equivalent. Some sectors—defense, dual-use, and enabling—are critical to national power and must be prioritized even at short-term economic cost.
Markets are indifferent to national power. Unregulated market forces will not automatically preserve strategic capabilities. Government must actively shape industrial structure through strategy, not just generic competitiveness or innovation policies.
China is a strategic competitor, not a normal trading partner. Chinese mercantilism requires defensive measures (restricting imports produced unfairly) and offensive support (strengthening domestic champions in national power industries) that violate free-market and progressive orthodoxies.
Production matters as much as innovation. The United States cannot rely on inventing technologies that China then produces. Manufacturing capabilities, supply chain resilience, and industrial commons must be preserved domestically in strategic sectors.
Long-term strategic positioning trumps short-term efficiency. Maintaining redundant capacity, subsidizing strategic industries, and accepting higher consumer prices are necessary costs of not losing the techno-economic war.
This requires jettisoning the deeply held view that governments should not “pick winners.” Markets might optimize GDP growth, but only by happenstance will this generate needed national power industry capabilities. Policymakers must embrace strategic industry selection and support, drawing on business strategy frameworks rather than consumer welfare economics.
The political economy obstacles to a national power industry strategy are severe. U.S. business leaders, shaped by decades of financial capitalism prioritizing quarterly returns and shareholder value, distrust government involvement and focus myopically on firm-level profitability rather than systemic strength. Unlike their predecessors from the 1940s–1970s who saw themselves as corporate statesmen with responsibilities to the broader capitalist system, today’s executives view government industrial policy as either incompetent interference or the thin edge of socialist control.
Labor unions pursue short-term wage gains that often undermine firms’ long-term global competitiveness because they are unable to escape the prisoner’s dilemma of aggressive bargaining today leading to job losses to less-constrained Chinese rivals tomorrow.
Conservative organizations reflexively oppose the government activism required for industrial strategy, while progressive organizations reflexively oppose supporting corporations. Neither party’s dominant coalition supports the combination of strong state capacity and empowered corporate champions that a national power industry strategy requires.
Perhaps most critically, the USG itself lacks the analytical capacity, institutional structures, and personnel with expertise to formulate and execute sophisticated industrial strategy. Unlike China, where officials study industrial policy as a discipline and spend careers mastering sectoral dynamics, U.S. policymakers typically have backgrounds in law or generalist economics divorced from operational understanding of specific industries and technologies.
The United States requires political, policy, and institutional transformation comparable to previous pivots after the War of 1812, the Civil War, and World War II. In all three cases, war provided the spur to overcome inertia and interest group resistance. We certainly hope it will not take a physical war to achieve similar transformation today. Either way, the organizing principle of economic policy must shift from maximizing consumer welfare or spurring social justice to ensuring that the United States maintains superior capabilities in national power industries relative to China. The simplest measures of this are the share of these industries’ global output that is produced in the United States and the share of U.S. production that occurs in allied nations. Related measures are the technological sophistication of U.S. products and services in national power industries compared with those of Chinese competitors.
The United States requires political, policy, and institutional transformation comparable to previous pivots after the War of 1812, the Civil War, and World War II.
This demands classifying industries by strategic importance, developing sophisticated strategies for priority sectors informed by business strategy principles rather than economics, restricting unfairly traded Chinese goods’ access to allied markets, substantially increasing public and private investment in strategic sectors (on the order of $100 billion per year in tax incentives and direct expenditures for at least a decade), coordinating with allies to present unified responses, and building government institutional capacity for industrial strategy.
The costs will be significant: Implementing a national power industry strategy will bring higher prices for certain consumer goods, increased government spending, greater fiscal discipline elsewhere, and reduced returns for some investors as capital is channeled toward strategic rather than merely profitable uses. But the alternative is worse: a future in which Chinese dominance of advanced industries leaves the United States dependent on an adversary for critical technologies, unable to defend its interests or protect its allies, and relegated to second-tier status in a China-dominated world order.
History shows that America can make fundamental pivots when circumstances demand. Whether it can do so absent the shock of military conflict—which might come too late, after critical capabilities are already lost—remains the defining question of our era. The window for effective action is narrowing. Chinese positions in industry after industry are becoming entrenched, protected by economies of scale, learning curves, network effects, and the enormous barriers to reentry that characterize advanced manufacturing. The reality is that once advanced industry capabilities are lost, they are extremely difficult to resurrect.
The choice facing America is stark and unavoidable: Fundamentally reform techno-economic policy now by embracing the uncomfortable truth that some industries matter far more than others—and by recognizing that preserving them requires active government strategy—or accept a managed decline into second-tier status while China’s techno-economic dominance translates into geopolitical supremacy. There is no third option, no magical innovation breakthrough that will solve the problem without hard choices and real sacrifices.
The United States remains far stronger than any declining power in history. Its advantages in innovation ecosystems, allied networks, capital markets, universities, and democratic legitimacy provide a foundation for successful competition if properly mobilized. But time is not on America’s side. Every industry lost makes recovery harder; every year of Chinese industrial expansion shifts the balance further; every failure to act because it violates free-market or progressive orthodoxies surrenders ground that cannot be regained. The techno-economic war with China is the central challenge of the 21st century. America’s response will determine not just its own future but the future of the liberal democratic world.

香港财政司长称香港金融贸易正从数量转向价值中国劳工公告栏
星期日, 15 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港及中国劳工新闻（英文）
香港财政司长表示城市金融贸易从数量转向价值
香港财政司司长陈茂波表示，香港金融和贸易正在从数量积累转向价值提升。他指出，离岸人民币债券目前占香港上市债券的38%，首次超过美元债券。陈还强调了机遇
香港财政司司长陈茂波表示，随着全球碎片化为更高价值的服务创造了机会，香港的金融和贸易部门正在从数量积累转向价值提升。
陈先生在11月15日的每周博客中写道，被称为“点心债券”的离岸人民币债券今年增长迅速。前三季度，它们占香港上市债券总数的38%，首次超过美元债券。发行主体变得更加多元化，包括内地科技公司、海外政府和金融机构。
陈表示，香港交易及结算所（港交所）将于11月16日推出离岸人民币债券指数，这是该交易所首个债券指数，涵盖在香港上市的300多只离岸人民币债券。他表示，该指数将为不断增长的点心债券市场提供基准。
陈将离岸人​​民币的更广泛使用归因于实际贸易需求，因为企业和投资者在地缘政治紧张和保护主义抬头​​的情况下寻求分散风险。
谈到航运，陈表示，随着绿色转型和人工智能重塑该行业，全球贸易模式正在发生变化。今年前10个月，替代燃料船舶订单同比增长近60%，但全球只有约25个港口能够供应甲醇，基础设施远远落后于需求。陈先生表示，这是香港国际航运中心从数量升级到价值的机遇。
陈说，政府不仅关注集装箱吞吐量，还关注更高价值的航运服务，如融资、保险、船舶管理、燃料供应、调解和仲裁。香港港口效率高，深海集装箱船平均停留时间仅为一天，仅为全球主要港口平均水平的一半，是国际航运重要的“省时港口”。该市的发展战略是将这种效率优势转化为服务优势。

Hong Kong finance chief says city shifting from quantity to value in finance and trade | China Labour Bulletin Board
Sunday, 15 Nov 2026 · Hong Kong Hong Kong and China labour news in English
Hong Kong finance chief says city shifting from quantity to value in finance and trade
Hong Kong's Financial Secretary Paul Chan said the city is moving from accumulating quantity to enhancing value in finance and trade. He noted that offshore yuan bonds now account for 38% of Hong Kong-listed bonds, surpassing US dollar bonds for the first time. Chan also highlighted opportunities in
Hong Kong's Financial Secretary Paul Chan said the city's financial and trade sectors are shifting from accumulating quantity to enhancing value, as global fragmentation creates opportunities for higher-value services.
Writing in his weekly blog on 15 November, Chan said offshore yuan bonds, known as "dim sum bonds", have grown rapidly this year. In the first three quarters, they accounted for 38 per cent of all bonds listed in Hong Kong, surpassing US dollar bonds for the first time. Issuers have become more diverse, including mainland technology firms, overseas governments and financial institutions.
Chan said Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) will launch an offshore yuan bond index on 16 November, the exchange's first bond index, covering more than 300 offshore yuan bonds listed in Hong Kong. He said the index would provide a benchmark for the growing dim sum bond market.
Chan attributed the wider use of the offshore yuan to real trade demand, as businesses and investors seek to diversify risk amid geopolitical tensions and rising protectionism.
Turning to shipping, Chan said global trade patterns are changing, with green transition and artificial intelligence reshaping the industry. In the first 10 months of this year, orders for alternative-fuel vessels rose nearly 60 per cent year-on-year, but only about 25 ports worldwide can supply methanol, leaving infrastructure far behind demand. Chan called this a chance for Hong Kong's international shipping centre to upgrade from quantity to value.
The government, Chan said, is focusing not just on container throughput but on higher-value shipping services such as financing, insurance, vessel management, fuel supply, mediation and arbitration. Hong Kong's port is efficient, with deep-sea container vessels staying an average of only one day, half the global average for major ports, making it an important "time-saving port" for international shipping. The city's development strategy is to turn this efficiency advantage into a service advantage.

content:
香港部长警告人工智能放缓可能会影响贸易，敦促自力更生中国劳工公告栏
星期日, 15 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港及中国劳工新闻（英文）
香港部长警告人工智能放缓可能影响贸易，敦促自力更生
香港商务主管表示，在人工智能相关电子产品贸易的推动下，9 月份出口同比飙升 64.9%。他警告全球人工智能发展可能放缓，并敦促香港寻找新机遇，而不是被动等待。
香港商业和经济发展部长表示，香港9月份出口同比飙升64.9%，为40多年来最快的月度增长，而进口则增长57.8%。
商务及经济发展局局长姚德华在电台节目中形容这些数字“令人印象深刻”，并表示增长主要是由与人工智能（AI）相关的电子产品贸易推动的。
姚指出，转口贸易对香港至关重要，并将其描述为“压舱石”。他表示，国家“十五五”规划要求香港巩固和提升国际贸易枢纽和国际航空枢纽地位。
部长警告，香港受全球格局影响，不同国家对人工智能发展有不同看法。他表示，未来人工智能发展可能会放缓，并强调香港“不能坐等好运降临”，必须自力更生，不断探索新机遇。

Hong Kong minister warns AI slowdown may hit trade, urges self-reliance | China Labour Bulletin Board
Sunday, 15 Nov 2026 · Hong Kong Hong Kong and China labour news in English
Hong Kong minister warns AI slowdown may hit trade, urges self-reliance
Hong Kong's commerce chief says September exports surged 64.9 per cent year-on-year, driven by AI-related electronics trade. He warns global AI development may slow and urges Hong Kong to find new opportunities rather than wait passively.
Hong Kong's September exports surged 64.9 per cent year-on-year, the fastest monthly growth in more than 40 years, while imports rose 57.8 per cent, the city's commerce and economic development minister has said.
Speaking on a radio programme, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Edward Yiu described the figures as “impressive” and said the growth was mainly driven by trade in electronic products related to artificial intelligence (AI).
Yiu noted that re-export trade is crucial for Hong Kong, describing it as a “ballast point”. He said the national 15th Five-Year Plan requires Hong Kong to consolidate and enhance its status as an international trading hub and international aviation hub.
The minister warned that Hong Kong is affected by the global landscape, and different countries have different views on AI development. He said future AI development may slow down, stressing that Hong Kong “cannot wait for luck to come” but must be self-reliant and continuously explore new opportunities.

title: Pact on South China Sea code of conduct unlikely, as ASEAN leaders gather
zh_title: 东盟领导人齐聚一堂，不太可能就南海行为准则达成协议
source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News a
summary: 东盟领导人齐聚一堂，不太可能就南海行为准则达成协议东盟 |半岛电视台 2024 年 3 月 5 日，东盟领导人在社交媒体上齐聚，不太可能就南海行为准则达成共识 2024 年 3 月 5 日，菲律宾补给船 Unaizah 在试图进入有争议的南海仁爱礁时，遭到中国海警水炮爆炸。“行为准则”协议尚未达成 [文件：Aaron Favila/美联社]东南亚国家（东盟）和中国正在有争议的南中国海制定“行为准则”
content:
东盟领导人齐聚一堂，不太可能就南海行为准则达成协议东盟 |半岛电视台
东盟领导人齐聚社交媒体，不太可能达成南海行为准则
2024 年 3 月 5 日，菲律宾补给船 Unaizah 5 月 4 日在试图进入有争议的南海仁爱礁时遭到中国海警水炮爆炸。“行为准则”协议尚未达成一致 [文件：Aaron Favila/美联社]
分析人士和官员表示，东南亚国家联盟（ASEAN）与中国之间期待已久的关于有争议的南海“行为准则”的协议不太可能在本周于马尼拉举行的地区集团领导人年度聚会期间实现。
该协议旨在控制紧张局势并防止海上冲突。但谈判已经拖延了20多年。 2023年，各国外交部长同意努力在三年内敲定该协议。
这个最后期限是 2026 年——这一年菲律宾轮流担任东盟主席国。外交部（DFA）表示，在其领导下，谈判代表每月至少举行一次会议。
但他们未能在峰会前达成共识。
外交部秘书玛丽亚·特蕾莎·拉扎罗周六表示：“我只想说，目前该文件本身已经完成了 80%。”她补充说，仍有一些“突出”要点需要解决。
她此前曾表示，地理范围是有争议的问题之一。北京坚称其对几乎整个南海拥有管辖权，尽管 2016 年的国际裁决宣告这一主张无效。
菲律宾、越南、马来西亚、文莱和印度尼西亚也有重叠的领土主张。
在菲律宾海岸警卫队提供的这张照片中，一艘中国海警船（右）于 2025 年 10 月 12 日向南海中业岛（当地称为 Pag-asa 岛）附近的菲律宾 BRP Datu Pagbuaya 发射水炮 [菲律宾海岸警卫队来自美联社/文件]
菲律宾外交部发言人多米尼克泽维尔帝国表示，菲律宾还希望该协议尊重该地区以外国家的权利。世界上一半的商船经过南海。
但这个国家可能会陷入进退两难的境地。
“你无法赢得它，因为如果你得到一份好的文件，你就会被指责为铁路，或者会被认为是自私自利。但如果这是一份糟糕的文件，小马科斯政府将被视为一个软弱的政府，”菲律宾大学政治学家阿里斯·阿鲁盖(Aries Arugay)表示。
中国一直指责美国及其盟国干涉定期与菲律宾进行航行自由行动。
自2022年菲律宾总统小费迪南德·马科斯上任以来，马尼拉和北京之间的紧张局势升级。中国海警多次对菲律宾船只部署高压水枪，海上对抗导致发生碰撞，甚至一度导致一名菲律宾士兵失去一根手指。
最近几周，两国一直在进行口水战。
9 月，菲律宾国防部长吉尔伯托·特奥多罗 (Gilberto Teodoro) 对一份拒绝 2016 年南海裁决的手写照会的公开回应（据报道来自北京驻首尔武官）迅速走红。
“也许基本的礼仪和行为才是中国需要做的，”被禁止进入中国的特奥多罗说。

【原文 English Original】
Pact on South China Sea code of conduct unlikely, as ASEAN leaders gather | ASEAN | Al Jazeera
Share Pact on South China Sea code of conduct unlikely, as ASEAN leaders gather on social media
The Philippine resupply vessel Unaizah May 4 is hit by a China Coast Guard water cannon blast as it tries to enter the Second Thomas Shoal in the disputed South China Sea, on March 5, 2024. A 'code of conduct' pact has yet to be agreed [File: Aaron Favila/AP]
A long-awaited pact between the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and China for a “code of conduct” in the disputed South China Sea is unlikely to materialise during the regional bloc’s annual gathering of leaders in Manila this week, analysts and officials say.
The agreement would aim to manage tensions and prevent conflict at sea. But talks have dragged on for more than 20 years. In 2023, foreign ministers agreed to work towards finalising the accord within three years.
That deadline fell on 2026 – the year the Philippines took its turn as chair of ASEAN. Under its leadership, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said negotiators have met at least once a month.
But they have fallen short of arriving at a consensus ahead of the summit.
“I just want to say that at this point in time, 80 percent of the document itself is finished,” DFA Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said on Saturday, adding that there are some ‘salient’ points that still need to be ironed out.
She has previously said that geographical scope is one of the contentious issues. Beijing insists it has jurisdiction over nearly the entire South China Sea despite a 2016 international ruling invalidating that claim.
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia also have overlapping territorial claims.
In this photo provided by the Philippine Coast Guard, a China Coast Guard vessel, right, fires its water cannon at the Philippines’ BRP Datu Pagbuaya near Thitu island, locally called Pag-asa island, in the South China Sea on October 12, 2025 [Philippine Coast Guard via AP/File]
The Philippines would also like the accord to respect the rights of countries outside the region, according to DFA spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial. Half of the world’s merchant ships pass through the South China Sea.
But the country may be caught between a rock and a hard place.
“You can’t win it because if you get a good document, you’ll be accused of railroading or it would come across as self-serving. But if it’s a bad document, the Marcos Jr administration will be seen as a weak government,” Aries Arugay, a political scientist at the University of the Philippines, said.
China has consistently accused the United States and its allies, who regularly conduct freedom of navigation operations with the Philippines, of interference.
Tensions between Manila and Beijing have escalated since Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in 2022. The China Coast Guard has repeatedly deployed water cannon against Philippine vessels and maritime confrontations have resulted in collisions and, on one occasion, a Filipino soldier losing a finger.
In recent weeks, the two countries have been engaged in a war of words.
In September, Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro’s public response to a handwritten note rejecting the 2016 South China Sea ruling – reportedly from Beijing’s military attache in Seoul – went viral.
“Perhaps basic decency and behaviour is what China needs to do,” Teodoro, who has been barred from entering China, said.
A month later, Beijing’s ambassador to Manila, Jing Quan, told reporters that if China wanted to use force, “we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force. We love peace”. The statement was made in response to a question about Teodoro calling China a “troublemaker”, but which Marcos said “sounded like a threat”.
What followed was a barrage of social media posts by Philippine officials criticising Jing, with the Chinese embassy replying in kind. Senators called for the expulsion of the Chinese envoy.
And, in late October, China accused Teodoro of a late invitation to the ASEAN defence ministers’ meeting in Cebu. Without ample time to prepare, it said it could only send its Manila-based defence attache.
“When that happened, I think the concern, especially on the part of the DFA, was, ‘We don’t want China not sending their premier. It would not look good on us as a host country,’” Lucio Pitlo, past president of the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies, said.
With just days before world leaders were due to arrive in Manila, diplomats from both sides stepped in.
In a phone call, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Lazaro, his Philippine counterpart, to rein in politicians.
“The Philippines should strengthen restraint over the relevant individuals and send a rational and unified voice on its policy toward China,” Wang said in a statement released by the Chinese embassy in Manila.
Lazaro described the conversation as having been “frank and constructive”.
However, the DFA followed up with a statement saying it found public commentary by certain government officials “regrettable”.
“Whatever personal convictions public officials may hold, their public platforms carry institutional responsibilities,” it said. “They may not pursue preferred approaches toward China, or any other international partner, without regard for the consequences on the government’s overall policy.”
Some analysts say the spat has further exposed division within the Marcos administration.
“They’re airing dirty laundry out there. It doesn’t communicate coherence. It doesn’t project a unified stance. This could have been an internal memo,” Arugay said.
But Pitlo said the last-ditch diplomatic effort had achieved its objective. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is now attending the ASEAN Leaders’ Summit in Manila.
Despite this, Pitlo shares pessimism about leaders reaching a conclusion to negotiations for a code of conduct in the South China Sea.
“I think with all the concerns about trade protectionism, the disruption in supply chains, economic issues will be very high in the agenda. I think it will be a tall order to get the code of conduct done.”

 The UK will buy three counter-mine "motherships" from Norway under a new agreement. (UK Ministry of Defence)

MILAN — The UK this week formalized plans to purchase three new mine-hunting “motherships” that can deploy unmanned mine countermeasure assets, as part of a defense cooperation agreement with Norway.

Under the UK-Norway Lunna House [Agreement](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-norway-lunna-house-agreement-on-defence), signed last December, the British government announced its intention to join the Norwegian P1118 Standardized Vessel Program to develop offshore support vessels as motherships for autonomous mine-hunting systems.

The decision, for which £90 million ($119.1 million) has been allocated, was [formalized](https://www.royalnavy.mod.uk/news/2026/november/12/20261112-royal-navy-agrees-export-deal-for-new-mine-hunting-motherships) on Thursday by British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting and his Norwegian counterpart, Tore O. Sandvik, at the Atlantic Future Forum in Oslo.

“This deal strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy …[We are] using the biggest sustained increase in defense spending since the Cold War to put the latest modern technology in the hands of our sailors,” Streeting said.

The British Ministry of Defense [said](https://www.royalnavy.mod.uk/news/2026/november/12/20261112-royal-navy-agrees-export-deal-for-new-mine-hunting-motherships) the vessels, built on the same family as Norway’s naval version of the P1118 design, will help keep sailors “further from danger” and, as a result, support “anti-submarine warfare capabilities on NATO’s northern flank.”

The first ship is expected to arrive in 2031, and the deal includes an option for London to order three more.

The threat posed by naval mines, especially in the Strait of Hormuz, has surged since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran launched mine-laying operations to restrict navigation of the waterway. In Thursday’s announcement, the British MoD [called](https://www.royalnavy.mod.uk/news/2026/november/12/20261112-royal-navy-agrees-export-deal-for-new-mine-hunting-motherships) these operations “illegal.” It said they caused “major disruption to the global trade in energy,” adding that the new mine-hunting capabilities will help the UK stay ahead of this threat.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

 Cover image: © France 24

01:39

Both the FAA and Microsoft said there were no signs that malicious activity had been behind the troubles.

Tori Perkins, 34, was hoping for a Saturday flight at Terminal 2 at San Diego International Airport, where 11 of the 62 flights already were listed as canceled that morning and the same number were delayed. Crowds were normal.

“It’s one of those things where I don’t necessarily believe what the [government](https://www.france24.com/en/tag/government/) says,” said Perkins, who seemed to take the setback in stride. “I don’t know what’s true because there are so many people saying different things.”

Perkins, who lives in Hawaii, was in San Diego on a layover on her way to see family in Florida. She spent Friday night at the airport.

She was not surprised that Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy had made a plea Friday for tens of billions in more funding to upgrade the country’s notoriously outdated air traffic system.

“It sounds like more of the same,” she said.

Read more[Passengers face further disruption as US flights slowly resume after ground stop](https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20261113-us-air-travel-resumption-will-take-time-after-hours-long-stop)

The FAA has already replaced [thousands of copper wire connections](https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20261114-copper-wires-to-blame-for-us-flight-disruption-says-trump-administration) with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. The White House has been pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.

Sometimes chaos brings out the best in people.

Corbyn Wascher was stuck on the tarmac at Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours while heading back to Moline, Illinois, from Miami, where he had been at an education conference.

He said everyone was cordial on the plane, talking to one another and stretching their legs. He was impressed with the American Airlines staff, who handed out water, pretzels and biscotti snacks, though they were clearly under stress.

“The stewardesses were amazing,” said the 37-year-old high school teacher.

Back at the Newark airport, Caroline Ruiz had caught a few hours of sleep by a heating vent. She wasn’t sure what time it was as she waited for someone to bring her a meal she was promised after the cancellation of the first leg of her 24-hour trip to Australia. She hoped to get started later Saturday.

It was two days in a row, she noted, where she had been betrayed by technology.

Though maybe one of those days didn’t count as a betrayal.

“I kind of got a free day yesterday” because the Microsoft systems were down.

_(FRANCE 24 with AP)_

# USS North Dakota (SSN 784) Changes Homeport to Pearl Harbor

By Lt.j.g. Samantha Prewitt, Commander, Submarine Force, U.S. Pacific Fleet Public Affairs

 JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii–
Virginia-class fast-attack submarine USS North Dakota (SSN 784) arrived at its new home port of Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, Nov. 13, 2026. North Dakota completed an Extended Drydocking Selected Restricted Availability at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, in Kittery, Maine, before joining Submarine Squadron 1 as its sixth Virginia-class fast-attack submarine.

"The crew of North Dakota is excited to call Pearl Harbor our new home," said U.S. Navy Cmdr. Christopher Marolt, commanding officer, North Dakota. "Our Sailors have put forth herculean efforts to get through the shortest availability in Portsmouth Naval Shipyard history, all while managing a homeport change to a new submarine homeport. We are ready to integrate with Submarine Squadron 1 and reunite with our families.”

Following North Dakota's arrival to Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, the submarine’s crew earned the Retention Excellence award in 2024 and the Commander, Submarine Force Atlantic Battle Efficiency (“Battle E”) award in 2024 and 2025, recognizing the crew's superior readiness, performance, and efficiency.

"It is an honor to welcome the Sailors and families of North Dakota to Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam as the newest addition to the waterfront,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Christopher Hedrick, commodore, Submarine Squadron 1. "It is the dedication of this crew that brings this boat to life. We are proud to have you on the team, supporting our strategic advantage in the Pacific."

North Dakota, a Virginia-class fast-attack submarine, was commissioned Oct. 25, 2014, and is the second U.S. warship commissioned under the name North Dakota, the first being World War I-era battleship USS North Dakota (BB-29).

"Saying farewell to Portsmouth, New Hampshire, is bittersweet, as the community there has supported us tremendously throughout our maintenance and preparation period," said Marolt. "However, bringing a battle-tested, back-to-back Battle 'E' crew into the Pacific Fleet theater is an incredible honor. We carry the proud heritage of our namesake and our recent successes with us as we stand ready to project power and support our allies and partners in this vital region."

content:
罗姗娜·罗 (Rosanna Law) 称赞“星空交响曲”是具有里程碑意义的年度盛事中国劳工公告栏
星期日, 15 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港及中国劳工新闻（英文）
罗姗娜·罗 (Rosanna Law) 称赞“星空交响曲”是具有里程碑意义的年度盛事
香港文化局局长称赞这次户外音乐会取得了圆满成功。此次活动以港乐、新任指挥和钢琴家为主角，并配有烟花和光剑。由于天气恶劣，比赛从周五推迟。
文化体育及旅游局局长罗淑佩称赞“星空交响曲”户外音乐会是一次非常成功的里程碑式活动，并指出11月14日星期六晚上场馆爆满。
罗杰周日在社交媒体上发帖称，晴朗的天气和热闹的气氛让与会者可以坐在草地上享受野餐，并在香港管弦乐团（港乐）的表演中欣赏维多利亚港的景色。她强调了观众对乐团新任音乐总监塔尔莫·佩尔托科斯基（Tarmo Peltokoski）和年轻的本地钢琴家岑阿里斯托（Aristo Sham）的巨大期待。
罗指出，今年的节目以轻松、熟悉的经典曲目为各个年龄段的音乐爱好者带来深刻的共鸣，例如圣桑俏皮的《动物嘉年华》，由佩尔托科斯基和岑与多位港乐首席在两架钢琴上演奏。与会者还欣赏了《星球大战组曲》，佩尔托科斯基在乐曲的开头和结尾使用发光的光剑进行了指挥。
晚会以柴可夫斯基1812序曲的表演和壮观的烟花表演结束。由于香港天文台预报有大雨和狂风雷暴，原定于周五举行的音乐会已推迟至周六晚上在中环海滨活动空间举行。

Rosanna Law hails 'Symphony Under the Stars' as landmark annual event
Hong Kong's culture secretary praised the outdoor concert as a packed success. The event featured the HK Phil, a new director and a pianist, with fireworks and a lightsaber. It was postponed from Friday due to bad weather.
Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui has hailed the "Symphony Under the Stars" outdoor concert as a highly successful landmark event, noting that the venue was packed to capacity on Saturday night, 14 November.
In a social media post on Sunday, Law said the clear weather and lively atmosphere allowed attendees to sit on the grass, enjoy picnics, and take in views of Victoria Harbour alongside the performance by the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra (HK Phil). She highlighted the immense anticipation from the audience for the orchestra's new music director, Tarmo Peltokoski, and the young local pianist, Aristo Sham.
Law noted that this year's programme featured lighthearted, familiar classics that deeply resonated with music lovers of all ages, such as Saint-Saëns's playful The Carnival of the Animals, which was performed on two pianos by Peltokoski and Sham alongside several HK Phil principals. Attendees also enjoyed the Star Wars Suite, which Peltokoski conducted using a glowing lightsaber at the beginning and end of the piece.
The evening concluded with a performance of Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture, accompanied by a spectacular fireworks display. The concert, originally scheduled for Friday, had been postponed to Saturday night at the Central Harbourfront Event Space due to the Hong Kong Observatory's forecasts of heavy rain and squally thunderstorms.

华盛顿多年来一直在争论人工智能（AI）在核指挥和控制中的作用，并为中美关系的军事影响而苦恼。人工智能竞赛。它花更少的时间提出一个不同的问题：如果朝鲜领导人金正恩相信美国即将在通用人工智能领域获得强大、持久的优势，那么他的威慑计算将如何改变？
通用人工智能（AGI）——被定义为在认知任务中与人类表现相匹配的强大智能——可能会进一步破坏已经恶化的核威慑关系的稳定。较弱的非 AGI 能力可能会变得尤其成问题。朝鲜的核态势已经一触即发。如果美国获得通用人工智能或类似通用人工智能的能力，平壤可能会采取一种激进的“使用它或失去它”的心态，因为它担心第一次打击会消除其核武器能力并摧毁其领导层。
至关重要的是，美国实际获得 AGI 以及随后发展威慑无效能力，比朝鲜对美国能力和意图的看法更重要。由于平壤采取了咄咄逼人的核姿态，并对美国的意图持批评、偏执的态度，因此，即使在通用人工智能能力投入使用之前，局势也可能会急剧恶化。因此，应该更多地关注通用人工智能如何打破不对称威慑平衡，尤其是针对平壤。
如果通用人工智能的腾飞真正带来指数级增长，一连串的技术突破可能会刺激前所未有的经济增长和军事能力的扩张，有些人称之为代理战争。在这种情况下，具有通用人工智能能力的国家可能会迅速削弱（甚至消除）非通用人工智能国家的二次打击能力。这种技术飞跃将放大不幸的心理倾向，即在面临损失时变得更容易冒险，这被称为前景理论。
因此，在AGI起飞的情况下，非AGI核武器国家，尤其是实力较弱的国家，可能会担心在不久的将来他们将无法威慑AGI国家。因此，他们可以采取更具攻击性的姿态。当然，这并不是唯一的理性反应，但出于我们稍后将描述的原因，我们认为朝鲜更有可能以额外的侵略性做出反应，而不是通过生存、隐蔽和军控谈判寻求庇护。此外，如果递归自我改进能够实现超级人工智能（ASI）（定义为超越任何人类的能力），那么风险将变得更高，核决策时间将变得更加压缩。

Washington has spent years debating the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in nuclear command and control, and agonizing over the military implications of China-U.S. AI competition. It has spent far less time asking a different question: how will North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s deterrence calculus change if he believes the United States is on the verge of obtaining a powerful, enduring advantage in artificial general intelligence?
Artificial general intelligence (AGI) – defined as powerful intelligence matching human performance across cognitive tasks – could further destabilize nuclear deterrence relationships that are already deteriorating. Weaker, non-AGI powers could become especially problematic. North Korea’s nuclear posture is already on a hair trigger. If the United States obtains AGI or AGI-like capabilities, Pyongyang could adopt an aggressive “use it or lose it” mentality because it fears a first strike that eradicates its nuclear weapons capabilities and decapitates its leadership.
Critically, the United States’ actual acquisition of AGI and the subsequent development of deterrence-nullifying capabilities matters less than North Korea’s perceptions of U.S. capabilities and intent. Because Pyongyang has adopted an aggressive nuclear posture and espouses such a critical, paranoid view of U.S. intentions, the situation could spiral even before AGI capabilities are operational. More attention should therefore be paid to how AGI could upset asymmetric deterrence equilibria, especially vis-à-vis Pyongyang.
If AGI takeoff truly unlocks exponential growth, a cascade of technological breakthroughs could spur unprecedented economic growth and expansion in military capabilities that some have termed agentic warfare. Under this scenario, an AGI-capable power could rapidly erode, if not eliminate, the second strike capabilities of a non-AGI power. This technological leap would amplify the unfortunate psychological tendency to become more risk-prone when facing losses, called prospect theory.
Accordingly, under AGI takeoff, non-AGI nuclear weapons powers, especially the weaker ones, will likely fear a near-future wherein they will be unable to deter the AGI power. They could therefore adopt a more aggressive posture. Of course, this isn’t the only rational reaction, but for reasons we will describe later, we think North Korea is much more likely to respond with extra aggression than it is to seek refuge through survivability, concealment, and arms control negotiations. Moreover, if recursive self-improvement delivers artificial superintelligence (ASI), defined as capabilities exceeding any human, the stakes will become much higher and nuclear decision-making timelines will become even more compressed.
AGI consequences, timelines, and diffusion remain a subject of debate, and key AI breakthroughs may be a business cycle or more away, but the balance of evidence suggests huge capability increases are possible. If scaling laws continue to hold, capabilities will keep rising: announced U.S. AI computing capacity is projected to increase by 239 percent this year alone, according to Federal Reserve staff calculations based on Epoch AI data. By 2030, planned U.S. AI compute would be roughly 35 times mid-2025 levels.
While tech CEOs and investors are incentivized to hype AI advances, models are undeniably improving, and at an impressive rate; the newest models are even proving adept at operating in the physical world. For better and for worse, AI software and hardware capabilities are advancing rapidly. Even artificial intelligence experts themselves have expressed surprise at the pace of innovation and warned of the dangers of unrestricted development.
Strategic deterrence nullification would likely lag AGI by many years, but AI timelines are advancing far faster than most expected. North Korea’s force posture is already changing and new command-and-control safeguards – including human-in-the-loop commitments – may take years to agree upon and implement.
AGI attainment would usher in considerable geopolitical disruptions, including altering the nuclear balance-of-power. China and Russia are of special importance in any AGI scenario. China is a peer competitor of the United States, including in AI, and it possesses the world’s third largest nuclear arsenal; Russia possesses the world’s largest nuclear weapon arsenal (by volume) and continues to face off against the United States in Cold War-style proxy conflict. Either competitor could be incentivized to act aggressively if the U.S. is first to approach AGI attainment.
Nevertheless, the gravest AGI-related dangers may come from less-capable nuclear powers, especially North Korea. That’s because Pyongyang has adopted a uniquely aggressive and decentralized form of nuclear command and control, has an aggressive nuclear doctrine, suffers from severe technical and even geographic disadvantages, and it maintains a paranoid disposition towards the United States. Faced with the prospect of losing second strike capability, it could therefore choose to adopt an even riskier posture or operationalize half-baked tech into its nuclear command, control, and communications before the United States crosses the AGI threshold.
Nuclear stability requires mutual vulnerability. China and Russia are more likely to continue to hold the U.S. hostage via threat of retaliation even if the U.S. obtains AGI first; for North Korea, that is much less likely.
AGI Takeoff, or Perceived Takeoff, Upends Conventional and Strategic Military Calculations
If AGI takeoff occurs, its technological, economic, and military consequences will be extremely hard to forecast. Physical constraints and hardware bottlenecks, including in critical minerals, could slow the transformation of software breakthroughs into weapons. Still, powerful AI could rapidly deliver unprecedented economic and technological capacity, which would then translate into military capabilities, including early warning, detection, targeting, and delivery. These capabilities could credibly threaten other states’ second-strike forces.
As the decision window shrinks, mutual vulnerability – the foundation of a stable deterrence relationship – will erode. Given the dangers of facing an AGI-empowered rival, and their own weak monitoring and verification capabilities, non-AGI powers like Pyongyang will watch anxiously for signs that an adversary’s AGI attainment could unlock the potential for a decapitation strike that wipes out their leadership and nuclear capabilities in one fell swoop.
In this scenario, facing rapidly deteriorating strategic options, a state could be motivated to automate nuclear retaliation. They might hope that the dead man’s hand would serve as a final guarantor of deterrence. But as human operators are pulled further out of the nuclear decision-making process, the ethical and practical problems will begin to multiply. History has proven that humans are the last best defense against needless escalation. That was the case in 1983 when a Soviet early warning system erroneously signaled an incoming U.S. intercontinental ballistic missile. Using his knowledge of the faulty system and U.S. strategy, Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov deduced that the warning was a false positive. He was right: the system’s satellites misread sunlight reflecting off clouds.
In addition, North Korea – and other non-AGI actors – might seek to establish deterrence via other asymmetric methods, such as pre-positioning chemical and biological weapons or developing new, AI-enabled variants. North Korea is thought to have a substantial inventory of both chemical and biological weapons, and it might lean on these capabilities if it fears its nuclear deterrent is compromised.
To limit near-term biological risks from Pyongyang, both Washington and Beijing should closely examine the AI-biology nexus, an asymmetrical threat that North Korea might find compelling to develop if it believed a rival was on the cusp of AGI acquisition. Limiting the risk of North Korea – or other state and non-state actors – may require constraining the publicly-accessible biological capabilities of future releases of large language models. Unsafeguarded models, known as open-weight models, pose the most severe risks. As unsafeguarded models become more capable, virtually anyone can access powerful, unconstrained AI by removing safeguards with relatively little compute.
North Korea is already likely operating unsafeguarded models to exploit zero-day vulnerabilities, as the $6 billion Binance hack suggests. Given the growing risks of AI-designed viruses, including from Pyongyang, Beijing and Washington should have candid conversations about the desirability of diffusing powerful AI capabilities in biology.
North Korea Is Uniquely Vulnerable and Aggressive
Unlike China or Russia, which have large nuclear arsenals, mature intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities, and demonstrated technological ability to innovate, North Korea’s vulnerability and its aggressive posture may render it the most dangerous nuclear actor in an AGI sprint scenario. Furthermore, unlike China or Russia, countries that can rely on second-strike deterrents due to their deep interiors and nuclear-armed submarines, North Korea lacks a credibly survivable nuclear submarine deterrent.
Finally, North Korea’s own eagerness to adopt AI-enabled weapons will color its perception of adversary intent and the threat posed by AGI. The nuclear deterrence equilibrium on the Korean Peninsula is already fragile; inviting one more destabilizing element may be the straw that breaks the camel’s back.
North Korea’s military is embracing AI with a speed that suggests it is throwing caution to the wind. In 2024, the General Staff Department of the Korean People’s Army created an Electronic Warfare and AI Operation Command to develop and adopt “AI-based electronic warfare support systems.” In August 2025, the Korean People’s Army issued orders to its Strategic Force to “integrate AI-based unified management systems for storing, operating, and commanding nuclear weapons, as well as launching nuclear counterattacks,” according to Daily NK. At the Ninth Party Congress in February of this year, North Korea announced additional plans to integrate AI into its civil and military systems. Since then, even more developments have been announced.
Leader Kim Jong Un himself jumped behind the wheel of a mobile rocket launcher, claiming that the nuclear-capable 600-mm multiple rocket launcher (KN-25) features artificial intelligence in its guidance systems. One month later, Kim oversaw a test of AI-enabled attack and reconnaissance drones, saying, “unmanned equipment and artificial intelligence should be top-prioritized… in modernizing the armed forces.” In May, North Korean media claimed that the military tested a tactical cruise missile that utilizes artificial intelligence for target acquisition and terminal guidance. Despite this appetite for integrating AI across military technologies, limitations in hardware, data, and infrastructure will likely constrain the rollout. These limitations could also produce defects that imperil safeguards meant to stop an unintentional escalation spiral.
Further aggravating the situation, North Korea’s nuclear doctrine is uniquely aggressive and opaque. The country’s rubber stamp parliament passed legislation in 2022 that legitimizes preemptive nuclear attacks under certain conditions. The North will launch a nuclear attack “automatically and immediately” if Kim’s command is threatened, if “a fatal military attack” on critical targets is imminent, or if needed to reclaim “the initiative in war.” The law also outlined a delegative command authority: “Rather than await direct orders from Kim Jong Un, field commanders may now follow predetermined launch plans to release nuclear weapons.” These doctrinal reforms were reinforced by a 2026 constitutional revision that codified the decentralized command authority. Combined with a surge in the production and forward deployment of tactical nuclear weapons, these changes add coherence and credibility to Kim’s first-use strategy, which aims to achieve a maximum deterrence effect through aggression and ambiguity. However, the blurry red lines and threats of preemption are risky and escalatory.
An AGI scenario could lead to further brinksmanship. As Keir A. Lieber and Daryl G. Press noted in a 2017 analysis, “The New Era of Counterforce,” states facing wealthy, technologically advanced adversaries will find it “increasingly difficult to secure their arsenals” as advances in sensors, data processing, and AI erode the conditions that have historically protected second-strike forces.
Pyongyang cannot rule out that an AGI-powered United States will develop next-generation technologies, such as airborne directed energy weapons, highly effective anti-ballistic missile defense, and orbital and sub-orbital weapons. Pyongyang’s weak early warning and intelligence capabilities will amplify the leadership’s fear that its second strike has been rendered moot, especially given its unique vulnerabilities. Nor can Washington easily reassure North Korea: even if the United States integrates AI cautiously into its own nuclear command, control, and communications and is transparent about human-in-the-loop safeguards, a leadership this distrustful could conclude that the AGI moment has arrived and act accordingly.
It is possible that, faced with such daunting odds, North Korea could choose a path of survivability, restraint, and even reconciliation. That would be a rational reaction to this newfound unfavorable position. However, given Pyongyang’s nuclear posture, its historical record, and the leadership’s consistent commitment to robust nuclear capabilities, it is much more likely that Pyongyang will double down on its “escalate to de-escalate” doctrine by adopting even riskier and more aggressive measures.
Fearing a super-capable U.S. and preoccupied with the threat of a decapitation strike, Pyongyang could be more likely to accept the downstream risks that come from adding AI-enabled processes. The first effort would be into their own nuclear command, control, and communications architecture, including early warning systems, targeting, command, control, communications, and navigation. Given North Korea’s already aggressive and risky posture, this embrace of AI can only increase the likelihood that an accidental clash could spiral into a full-on nuclear exchange. In addition, any attack on the North Korean infrastructure supporting the Korean People’s Army AI electronic warfare systems could be interpreted as a nuclear-level aggression, leading to a nuclear-level reprisal.
The efficacy of AI systems is limited by the quality of training data, sensory input, and processing power. In North Korea’s case, the quality of all three is extremely limited. This could produce false positives, which become exponentially more dangerous as humans are removed from the decision-making process. Pairing super-compressed decision timelines with automated attack protocols makes it difficult for a cool-headed human to steer the situation away from crisis. That’s doubly the case when the two states in question lack diplomatic relations, crisis communications, or confidence building measures.
Contrary to popular depictions – including Annie Jacobsen’s book “Nuclear War: A Scenario” and Kathryn Bigelow’s 2025 film “A House of Dynamite” – North Korea’s leadership understands well that launching a pre-emptive strike would be suicidal. But the alarming truth is that Pyongyang could make much more subtle and obscure posture changes that would dramatically increase the chance of accidental escalation. Facing an AGI-enabled United States, North Korea would be much more likely to hastily operationalize half-baked AI nuclear command, control, and communications, hedge with chemical and biological weapons, forward deploy additional assets, engage in gray zone attacks, and engage in aggression that blurs the line between nuclear testing and use, such as an atmospheric test near Korea or Japan that produces no casualties. They may also expand the list of red line items that trigger field commanders to independently launch a nuclear strike.
The United States faces a complex optimization problem: staying ahead of Chinese AI development while managing the nuclear deterrence instability that AGI could unleash, and the potential existential risks of AI itself. Policymakers should begin examining and counteracting these risks now, instead of scrambling in a takeoff scenario. Constraining Chinese access to advanced semiconductors is necessary but not sufficient. U.S. policymakers must also consider how their own AGI development will affect deterrence calculus in other capitals and explore voluntary restraints on capabilities that would destabilize fragile nuclear equilibria.
The next frontier of arms control should include a “human in the loop” clause such as the one featured in the 2024 agreement between the United States and China. The U.S. should lead a multilateral effort to secure buy in from all nuclear powers to commit to the same provisions and more – to wall off as much higher-function nuclear command, control, and communications from automaticity as possible. While it may seem counter-intuitive to consider that Pyongyang would accept limitations on its nuclear program, participation in such a multilateral agreement with the world’s nuclear powers might actually bestow upon it the kind of international legitimacy that Kim craves. And this sort of legitimacy is categorically different from prior offerings because it would situate North Korea among nuclear superpowers on an equitable basis, a tantalizing prospect for Kim that cannot be easily dismissed.
While some may criticize such an effort on the grounds of creating a dangerous precedent by tacitly accepting Pyongyang’s nuclear status, the time has come to stop tilting at “denuclearization” windmills in favor of achieving a material threat reduction, as one of us has argued previously. To be sure, convincing the distrustful leadership in Pyongyang to voluntarily accept limitations on its nuclear program will not be an easy sell. But the costs of inaction are so high and the alternatives so disagreeable that, in the land of lousy policy options, this is an endeavor worthy of focus, energy, and political capital.
Beijing could play a role in containing nuclear-related and asymmetric biological risks. Given the risks of powerful AI diffusing biological research capabilities, and enabling an asymmetric counter to AGI, both the U.S. and China have an interest in constraining AI’s publicly-accessible biological capabilities. The same applies to limiting North Korea’s nuclear capabilities. As during the Six Party Talks, Beijing should be recruited to support Pyongyang’s engagement and implementation.
Over time, such a framework could begin to eat away at the distrust that fuels North Korea’s paranoia and spurs its aggressive nuclear posture. If Kim Jong Un continues to reject good faith efforts, then the U.S. and its allies South Korea and Japan should invest substantially and collaboratively on missile defense architecture and other capabilities needed to address the threat and maintain deterrence. That consequence should incentivize China to act responsibly.
